screens.title: The java.nio.file API: Modern File I/O
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore java. nio. file, the modern input and output A P I introduced in Java 7 that replaces many of the weaknesses of the older java. io. File approach. You will learn why Path and Files form a cleaner separation of concerns: Path models a file system path as an immutable object, while Files supplies powerful, static operations for creation, reading, writing, copying, and traversing. We will work through concrete examples that create directories, write and read text, copy and delete files, and list directory contents both non-recursively and recursively. You will also see why NIO.2 gives better error information through specific exceptions, how symbolic links affect traversal, and how atomic options can prevent partial writes or moves. By the end you should be comfortable choosing Path over File, using Files methods with appropriate options, and writing safer, clearer file input and output code. Think about a small project where you need reliable backup and traversal — NIO.2 makes that task explicit and testable.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

The java.nio.file API: Modern File I/O

Adopt object-oriented path values and the Files utility to perform reliable, expressive file system operations. This chapter focuses on practical code and safe patterns for creating, reading, traversing, and cleaning up files and directories.

In this lesson
Path and Files essentials

Learn Path, Files, basic ops, traversal, and exceptions with code examples.

Coming up
Directory traversal

Use Files.list and Files.walk safely, and understand FileVisitor for custom traversal.

Hands-on
ProjectManager demo

A guided code walk through creating a project structure and processing files.

Why this matters
Reliable file I/O prevents data loss, enables clear error handling, and integrates with streams and attributes for modern Java applications.
Concept Map
Paths → Files → Traversal
Path: immutable path value, resolve/normalize
Files: static operations, read/write/copy/move
Traversal: Files.list, Files.walk, FileVisitor
Quick example
Path p = Paths.get("docs", "readme.md");
Files.createDirectories(p.getParent());
Files.write(p, List.of("Hello"), StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
This short snippet shows creating parent directories then writing text using Files.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives focus your practice and assessment. First, you'll understand why java. nio. file was introduced and how it fixes concrete limitations of java. io. File, improving error reporting and supporting symbolic links and attributes. Second, you will be able to construct and manipulate Path objects with methods like resolve, normalize, and toAbsolutePath so your code treats paths as immutable, testable values. Third, you'll perform common operations using Files: create directories, write and read bytes or lines, copy, move, and delete resources while choosing options such as REPLACE_EXISTING or ATOMIC_MOVE for safety. Fourth, you'll explore robust traversal techniques with Files. list, Files. walk, and Files. walkFileTree, and handle exceptions like NoSuchFileException and AccessDeniedException precisely. Each objective includes a short skill and why it matters: better diagnostics, safer input and output, clearer code, and reliable traversal. Practically, you will apply these with the provided ProjectManager hands-on code, which is a small clean-up-safe project that creates, lists, processes, and deletes a sample project folder.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Practice Skills
Hands-on skills
Create dirs
Files.createDirectories(path) creates parent folders as needed and is idempotent when directory exists.
Write & read
Files.write and Files.readAllLines/Files.readAllBytes for text and binary operations; choose based on file size.
Copy & move
Use StandardCopyOption to replace or request atomic moves when supported by the file system.
Traversal
Files.list for shallow listings; Files.walk or FileVisitor for recursive control and filtering with streams.
Check your understanding
When should you use Files.readAllBytes instead of readAllLines? Consider file size and binary vs text semantics. What exceptions will help you detect missing files versus access problems?
Mnemonic
Think: Path = value, Files = verbs. Path builds and describes; Files acts on it.
This mental model prevents mixing responsibilities and helps you reason about atomic operations and exception handling.

screens.title: Why java.nio.file replaces java.io.File
screens.narratorSegment: For years java. io. File was the de facto file A P I in Java. It worked for many simple tasks but mixed responsibilities: a File instance combined path name handling and file operations. Methods often returned boolean, which makes diagnosing failures difficult because you lose the exception context. NIO.2 splits responsibilities: Path represents an immutable path value, and Files provides static operations. This design yields several practical advantages. First, you get richer error information because Files methods throw specific exceptions such as NoSuchFileException or FileAlreadyExistsException — that helps you provide clearer recovery or messaging logic. Second, NIO.2 brings explicit support for symbolic links and file attributes, so code can inspect or skip links with LinkOption. NOFOLLOW_LINKS. Third, atomic operations like ATOMIC_MOVE reduce the chance of partial updates on move or copy operations when the file system supports them. As a concrete example, imagine replacing a configuration file: with Files. move and ATOMIC_MOVE you avoid leaving a partial file if the operation is interrupted. A common misconception is thinking Path replaces File's semantics exactly — it doesn't. Path is a value describing a location; you still need Files methods to act. The takeaway: prefer Path and Files for clearer, safer, and more expressive file input and output.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Why NIO.2
Problem with java.io.File
  • Methods often returned boolean, hiding reason for failure.
  • File mixed path representation with file operations.
  • Lacked built-in support for attributes and symbolic links.
NIO.2 advantages
  • Path is an immutable path value with manipulation helpers.
  • Files provides static verbs with specific exceptions.
  • Support for atomic operations, links, attributes, and stream-friendly traversal.
Concrete example
Replacing a configuration file safely:
Path src = Paths.get("config.tmp");
Path dest = Paths.get("config.properties");
Files.move(src, dest, StandardCopyOption.ATOMIC_MOVE, StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING);
Common mistake
Mixing File and Path in the same module can cause confusion; prefer one API per code path and use conversion methods if necessary.
Key Takeaway

NIO.2 separates path representation from file actions, enabling clearer error handling and modern file system features.

screens.title: Path: immutable, composable file system values
screens.narratorSegment: Path is the central abstraction in NIO.2: an immutable object that models a file or directory location. It does not guarantee the file exists — it simply describes a location to operate on. You obtain Path instances using Paths. get with path segments, which produces platform-aware Path values. Common instance methods let you compose and inspect paths: resolve will append a child segment to a parent path, getParent returns the containing directory, getFileName returns the last element, toAbsolutePath yields an absolute path, and normalize removes redundant name elements. For example, Paths. get("docs", "../reports", "summary. txt"). normalize() will collapse the parent reference so the path is predictable. A common pitfall is assuming Path operations perform input and output — they do not. Path. normalize() and resolve() just manipulate the value. You must call Files methods to create or check a resource. Practically, treat Path like a string with helper methods: use it to compute destinations, validate names, and then call Files operations with explicit options. This separation allows testable logic for path construction without touching the file system during unit tests.

keyIdea.title: Path as value
keyIdea.text: Use Path to build and inspect file system locations without performing I/O; call Files methods when you want side effects.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Path Basics
Constructing Paths
Path p1 = Paths.get(".");
Path p2 = Paths.get("documents", "report.txt");
Path p3 = Paths.get("/home/user/data/config.json");
Paths.get accepts multiple segments and returns a Path tailored to the platform. No I/O occurs yet.
Useful methods
  • resolve(): append child segments
  • getParent(), getFileName()
  • toAbsolutePath(), normalize()
Example: compute a file location
Use resolve and normalize to create reliable destination paths before performing I/O:
Path base = Paths.get("project");
Path report = base.resolve("../project-reports").resolve("2024/report.txt");
Path normalized = report.normalize();
Misconception
Calling normalize or resolve performs file system changes — it does not. Only Files methods interact with the disk.
Key Takeaway

Treat Path as a testable value for building file locations; separate computation from effects.

screens.title: Files: the utility class that performs file system operations
screens.narratorSegment: Files is a static utility class that contains nearly all the verbs you need to operate on paths: create, copy, move, delete, read, and write. The A P I is designed so methods accept Path instances and, where appropriate, an options varargs to control behavior. For instance, Files. createDirectories will create missing parents; Files. delete throws an exception if the file is missing while Files. deleteIfExists is permissive. For copy and move there are StandardCopyOption flags such as REPLACE_EXISTING or ATOMIC_MOVE; the latter requests an atomic operation when supported by the filesystem. For reads and writes: Files. readAllLines returns a List of strings useful for small to medium text files; Files. readAllBytes returns raw bytes for binary data. Files. write can accept Iterable for text or a byte[] for binary. When designing code, select the methods that match your data size and semantics. A common mistake is using readAllBytes for very large files, which can cause memory pressure. Another mistake is blind use of delete without handling FileAlreadyExistsException or DirectoryNotEmptyException. The Files design makes these conditions explicit so you can respond appropriately.

keyIdea.title: Files is the action API

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Files API
Common Files operations
  • Existence checks: Files.exists(path), Files.notExists(path)
  • Create: Files.createFile, Files.createDirectory, Files.createDirectories
  • Delete: Files.delete, Files.deleteIfExists
  • Copy/Move: Files.copy, Files.move with CopyOption/StandardCopyOption
  • Read/Write: Files.readAllLines, Files.readAllBytes, Files.write
Choose the variant that matches your semantics: use deleteIfExists when deletion failures should not throw, and use REPLACE_EXISTING when you intend to overwrite.
Example: safe copy with replace
Path src = Paths.get("data.bin");
Path dst = Paths.get("backup", "data.bin");
Files.createDirectories(dst.getParent());
Files.copy(src, dst, StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING);
Pro tip
Use StandardCopyOption.ATOMIC_MOVE when you need an atomic replacement and the file system supports it. This avoids partial writes on interruption.
Key Takeaway

Files methods make intent explicit and provide options for safe behavior; pick the method and options to match your desired semantics.

screens.title: Reading and writing files: text and binary
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right read and write method matters for performance and correctness. For small and medium text files, Files. readAllLines(path, charset) returns a List that is convenient to process line-by-line. For binary data or when you need raw bytes, Files. readAllBytes(path) returns a byte array. Files. write accepts either an Iterable of strings for text or a byte[] for binary content. The important practical rule is: prefer readAllLines for human-readable files of modest size, readAllBytes only when you actually need raw bytes, and stream-based APIs for very large files. Let's work through a focused code example that appears in the chapter. The example creates a directory and writes a few lines to a text file, then reads them back and prints metadata like size and last modification time. This pattern demonstrates combining Files. createDirectories, Files. write with CREATE and TRUNCATE_EXISTING options, Files. readAllLines, and Files. size. A common misconception is assuming these methods are non-throwing; they can throw IOException and more specific subclasses, so structure your code to catch and respond to exceptions meaningfully. When reading back the content, check the file size and last-modified attributes to validate your operation.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Read & Write
Code example (excerpt)
Path subDir = baseDir.resolve("reports");
Path filePath = subDir.resolve("quarterly_summary.txt");

Files.createDirectories(subDir);
Files.write(filePath, lines, StandardCharsets.UTF_8, StandardOpenOption.CREATE, StandardOpenOption.TRUNCATE_EXISTING);

List readLines = Files.readAllLines(filePath, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
long size = Files.size(filePath);
FileTime lastModified = Files.getLastModifiedTime(filePath);
This snippet shows directory creation, writing lines with explicit charset and open options, then reading and checking attributes.
Practical guidance
  • Text files: prefer readAllLines for convenience.
  • Binary data: use readAllBytes or streams to preserve bytes.
  • Large files: use streaming APIs (Files.newBufferedReader, Files.newInputStream) to avoid loading all content into memory.
Common mistake
Using readAllBytes on very large files can exhaust memory. Choose streams for heavy data.
Key Takeaway

Match Files read/write methods to file size and format: text helpers for lines, byte helpers for binary, streams for large files.

screens.title: Directory traversal with Files.list and Files.walk
screens.narratorSegment: Traversing directories is a common task and NIO.2 provides several APIs tailored to different needs. Files. list(dir) returns a Stream of entries in a directory — it is non-recursive and useful when you only need the first level. Files. walk(start) returns a Stream that visits the start and its descendants recursively; you can supply a maxDepth to limit recursion. These Streams integrate with the Java 8 Streams A P I, so you can filter by file name, map to metadata, and collect results concisely. For example, Files. walk(start). filter(p -> p. toString(). endsWith(". java")) will yield all Java files beneath a tree. Streams returned by Files. list and Files. walk must be closed either explicitly or by using try-with-resources to avoid resource leaks. A common misconception is treating Files. walk as lazy without closing it; leaving the stream open can hold file handles. Another important point: when you need precise control or need to handle failures during traversal, use Files. walkFileTree with a FileVisitor implementation. Files. list is fast and simple for flat listings, Files. walk is concise for recursive needs, and both work well with streams-based filters and short-circuit operations.

keyIdea.title: Traversal choices
keyIdea.text: Use Files.list for shallow listings and Files.walk for recursive streams; always close streams or use try-with-resources to avoid leaks.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Directory Traversal
Files.list (shallow)
try (Stream entries = Files.list(dir)) {
  entries.filter(Files::isRegularFile)
         .forEach(p -> System.out.println(p.getFileName()));
}
Use for non-recursive directory reads. Remember to close the stream.
Files.walk (recursive)
try (Stream walk = Files.walk(start, 3)) {
  walk.filter(p -> p.toString().endsWith(".java"))
      .forEach(System.out::println);
}
Files.walk produces a recursive stream; supply maxDepth or filter results to limit work. Use try-with-resources.
Why this matters
Stream-based traversal composes well with filters and collectors. Properly closing streams avoids leaking file handles and strange errors on some platforms.

screens.title: Files.walkFileTree and FileVisitor
screens.narratorSegment: Files. walkFileTree is the most flexible traversal A P I. It accepts a starting Path and a FileVisitor implementation. FileVisitor exposes callbacks: preVisitDirectory for logic before entering a directory, visitFile for each file, visitFileFailed for handling failures like permission issues, and postVisitDirectory for cleanup after visiting a directory. This callback model allows you to control traversal order, skip subtrees, or collect detailed metadata. For example, in a cleanup routine you might delete files as you visit them and then delete the now-empty directory in postVisitDirectory. Because callbacks receive IOException in failed visits, you can decide whether to continue or abort. A common misconception is that Stream-based walk can replace FileVisitor for all advanced needs; while Streams are concise, they lack the fine-grained lifecycle hooks and explicit failure handling that FileVisitor provides. Use walkFileTree when you need to atomically delete a non-empty directory or implement complex rules during traversal. The A P I is a bit more code, but it yields robust control for production scenarios like project cleanup or archival tasks. Files.walkFileTree and FileVisitor means use filevisitor with files.walkfiletree when you need controlled lifecycle callbacks and explicit failure handling during recursive traversal.. In practical terms, custom traversal with previsit, postvisit, and failure handling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Walk File Tree
FileVisitor callbacks
  • preVisitDirectory — before entering a directory
  • visitFile — for each file
  • visitFileFailed — when a file cannot be read
  • postVisitDirectory — after finishing a directory
Use these methods to control deleting order, skipping subtrees, or accumulating metadata safely.
Example pattern: delete tree
Files.walkFileTree(start, new SimpleFileVisitor<Path>() {
  @Override
  public FileVisitResult visitFile(Path file, BasicFileAttributes attrs) throws IOException {
    Files.delete(file);
    return FileVisitResult.CONTINUE;
  }

  @Override
  public FileVisitResult postVisitDirectory(Path dir, IOException exc) throws IOException {
    Files.delete(dir);
    return FileVisitResult.CONTINUE;

});

screens.title: Symbolic links, LinkOptions, and file attributes
screens.narratorSegment: Symbolic links are file system entries that point to other files or directories. In NIO.2 you can detect links with Files. isSymbolicLink(path) and control following behavior with LinkOption. NOFOLLOW_LINKS when calling some Files methods. This is important when traversing trees; following links blindly can create cycles or unexpected locations. File attributes such as size, last modified time, and permissions are accessible through Files. size, Files. getLastModifiedTime, and other attribute views. For example, you can call Files. getLastModifiedTime(path) to validate when a file changed, or use Files. isReadable to test permissions. Many Files methods accept LinkOption varargs so you explicitly state whether to follow links. A common pitfall is assuming isRegularFile or isDirectory will behave the same for links; those methods may follow the link unless you pass the NOFOLLOW_LINKS option. Also, attribute reads may throw IOException or AccessDeniedException when permissions block access, so design your code to handle those exceptions and fall back appropriately. Understanding links and attributes gives you safer traversal and more precise file handling. Symbolic links, LinkOptions, and file attributes means be explicit about following symbolic links and use attribute queries to validate file state while handling permission-related exceptions.. screens.title: Mixing File and Path — best practices and pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Although conversion methods exist between java. io. File and java. nio. file. Path (File. toPath and Path. toFile), mixing the two APIs in the same module can lead to confusion. File carries both path and state-like behavior, whereas Path is purely a value. When you call File methods you may get older semantics and weaker error signals. If your codebase already uses File extensively, prefer adopting Path and Files gradually: convert File instances to Path at module boundaries and migrate operations to Files. When converting, be mindful of differences: for example, File methods like renameTo have platform-dependent semantics and return booleans; Files. move throws specific exceptions and accepts options. A practical pattern is to centralize all file-system access in a utility class that uses Path and Files internally and exposes higher-level operations to the rest of your app. This reduces accidental use of outdated File semantics and makes it simpler to apply atomic options and precise exception handling consistently across code paths. The rule of thumb: prefer a single A P I per context and migrate tests to operate against Path-based utilities.

screens.title: Handling exceptions: specific I/O errors help recovery
screens.narratorSegment: NIO.2 provides a richer exception model than the old generic IOException pattern. Methods in Files commonly throw specific subclasses such as NoSuchFileException when a referenced path is missing, FileAlreadyExistsException when attempting to create a file that exists, AccessDeniedException when permissions prevent access, and DirectoryNotEmptyException when deleting a directory that still contains files. Catching specific exceptions enables precise recovery: prompt the user to create a missing file when you catch NoSuchFileException, or retry with different options when you encounter FileAlreadyExistsException. A common anti-pattern is catching Exception or IOException broadly and logging a generic message; that obscures the true cause. Structure your code to catch specific exceptions first and provide meaningful actions, then fall back to a broader catch for unexpected conditions. Also keep in mind that some operations can throw unchecked exceptions like SecurityException; consider permission boundaries, particularly in sandboxed contexts. Clear and specific exception handling improves user feedback and simplifies troubleshooting in production systems. screens.title: Atomic operations and safe copy/move patterns
screens.narratorSegment: When moving or copying critical files, partial updates can corrupt data. NIO.2 helps with StandardCopyOption flags. REPLACE_EXISTING makes intent explicit when you want to overwrite, while ATOMIC_MOVE requests the file system perform the move atomically — either the move completes fully or not at all — which is crucial when replacing critical assets. However, ATOMIC_MOVE requires file system support and may fail, so design fallback behavior. A safe pattern for replacing a file is: write to a temporary file in the same directory, then move the temporary file to the target using ATOMIC_MOVE with REPLACE_EXISTING. This reduces window for partial writes because the file object appearing at the final path happens atomically when supported. Also validate target permissions before the operation and catch FileAlreadyExistsException or AtomicMoveNotSupportedException to implement a fallback strategy. A common mistake is assuming ATOMIC_MOVE is always available; check for exceptions and document the fallback you provide. These patterns improve crash resilience and reduce corruption risk in production systems. Atomic operations and safe copy/move patterns means write to a temp file, then move it with atomic_move and replace_existing when supported to avoid partial updates and reduce corruption risk.. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore java. nio. file, the modern input and output A P I introduced in Java 7 that replaces many of the weaknesses of the older java. io. File approach. You will learn why Path and Files form a cleaner separation of concerns: Path models a file system path as an immutable object, while Files supplies powerful, static operations for creation, reading, writing, copying, and traversing. We will work through concrete examples that create directories, write and read text, copy and delete files, and list directory contents both non-recursively and recursively. You will also see why NIO.2 gives better error information through specific exceptions, how symbolic links affect traversal, and how atomic options can prevent partial writes or moves. By the end you should be comfortable choosing Path over File, using Files methods with appropriate options, and writing safer, clearer file input and output code. Think about a small project where you need reliable backup and traversal — NIO.2 makes that task explicit and testable.

These learning objectives focus your practice and assessment. First, you'll understand why java. nio. file was introduced and how it fixes concrete limitations of java. io. File, improving error reporting and supporting symbolic links and attributes. Second, you will be able to construct and manipulate Path objects with methods like resolve, normalize, and toAbsolutePath so your code treats paths as immutable, testable values. Third, you'll perform common operations using Files: create directories, write and read bytes or lines, copy, move, and delete resources while choosing options such as REPLACE_EXISTING or ATOMIC_MOVE for safety. Fourth, you'll explore robust traversal techniques with Files. list, Files. walk, and Files. walkFileTree, and handle exceptions like NoSuchFileException and AccessDeniedException precisely. Each objective includes a short skill and why it matters: better diagnostics, safer input and output, clearer code, and reliable traversal. Practically, you will apply these with the provided ProjectManager hands-on code, which is a small clean-up-safe project that creates, lists, processes, and deletes a sample project folder.

This second objectives screen zooms into practical skills you will practice. You will reliably create directories using Files. createDirectories, knowing it will make parent directories when necessary. You will create and write files with Files. write and read their contents with Files. readAllLines or Files. readAllBytes, choosing the method that matches file size and binary versus text handling. You will move and copy files with options like StandardCopyOption. REPLACE_EXISTING and ATOMIC_MOVE when the file system supports it to avoid partial state. You will build safe traversal code using Files. list for shallow views and Files. walk for recursive processing, and you will learn how to use FileVisitor when you need fine-grained control over pre-visit, post-visit, and failure handling. Finally, you will practice catching specific exceptions such as FileAlreadyExistsException and AccessDeniedException so your recovery behavior can be precise and user-friendly.

For years java. io. File was the de facto file A P I in Java. It worked for many simple tasks but mixed responsibilities: a File instance combined path name handling and file operations. Methods often returned boolean, which makes diagnosing failures difficult because you lose the exception context. NIO.2 splits responsibilities: Path represents an immutable path value, and Files provides static operations. This design yields several practical advantages. First, you get richer error information because Files methods throw specific exceptions such as NoSuchFileException or FileAlreadyExistsException — that helps you provide clearer recovery or messaging logic. Second, NIO.2 brings explicit support for symbolic links and file attributes, so code can inspect or skip links with LinkOption. NOFOLLOW_LINKS. Third, atomic operations like ATOMIC_MOVE reduce the chance of partial updates on move or copy operations when the file system supports them. As a concrete example, imagine replacing a configuration file: with Files. move and ATOMIC_MOVE you avoid leaving a partial file if the operation is interrupted. A common misconception is thinking Path replaces File's semantics exactly — it doesn't. Path is a value describing a location; you still need Files methods to act. The takeaway: prefer Path and Files for clearer, safer, and more expressive file input and output.

Path is the central abstraction in NIO.2: an immutable object that models a file or directory location. It does not guarantee the file exists — it simply describes a location to operate on. You obtain Path instances using Paths. get with path segments, which produces platform-aware Path values. Common instance methods let you compose and inspect paths: resolve will append a child segment to a parent path, getParent returns the containing directory, getFileName returns the last element, toAbsolutePath yields an absolute path, and normalize removes redundant name elements. For example, Paths. get("docs", "../reports", "summary. txt"). normalize() will collapse the parent reference so the path is predictable. A common pitfall is assuming Path operations perform input and output — they do not. Path. normalize() and resolve() just manipulate the value. You must call Files methods to create or check a resource. Practically, treat Path like a string with helper methods: use it to compute destinations, validate names, and then call Files operations with explicit options. This separation allows testable logic for path construction without touching the file system during unit tests.

Files is a static utility class that contains nearly all the verbs you need to operate on paths: create, copy, move, delete, read, and write. The A P I is designed so methods accept Path instances and, where appropriate, an options varargs to control behavior. For instance, Files. createDirectories will create missing parents; Files. delete throws an exception if the file is missing while Files. deleteIfExists is permissive. For copy and move there are StandardCopyOption flags such as REPLACE_EXISTING or ATOMIC_MOVE; the latter requests an atomic operation when supported by the filesystem. For reads and writes: Files. readAllLines returns a List of strings useful for small to medium text files; Files. readAllBytes returns raw bytes for binary data. Files. write can accept Iterable for text or a byte[] for binary. When designing code, select the methods that match your data size and semantics. A common mistake is using readAllBytes for very large files, which can cause memory pressure. Another mistake is blind use of delete without handling FileAlreadyExistsException or DirectoryNotEmptyException. The Files design makes these conditions explicit so you can respond appropriately.

Choosing the right read and write method matters for performance and correctness. For small and medium text files, Files. readAllLines(path, charset) returns a List that is convenient to process line-by-line. For binary data or when you need raw bytes, Files. readAllBytes(path) returns a byte array. Files. write accepts either an Iterable of strings for text or a byte[] for binary content. The important practical rule is: prefer readAllLines for human-readable files of modest size, readAllBytes only when you actually need raw bytes, and stream-based APIs for very large files. Let's work through a focused code example that appears in the chapter. The example creates a directory and writes a few lines to a text file, then reads them back and prints metadata like size and last modification time. This pattern demonstrates combining Files. createDirectories, Files. write with CREATE and TRUNCATE_EXISTING options, Files. readAllLines, and Files. size. A common misconception is assuming these methods are non-throwing; they can throw IOException and more specific subclasses, so structure your code to catch and respond to exceptions meaningfully. When reading back the content, check the file size and last-modified attributes to validate your operation.

Traversing directories is a common task and NIO.2 provides several APIs tailored to different needs. Files. list(dir) returns a Stream of entries in a directory — it is non-recursive and useful when you only need the first level. Files. walk(start) returns a Stream that visits the start and its descendants recursively; you can supply a maxDepth to limit recursion. These Streams integrate with the Java 8 Streams A P I, so you can filter by file name, map to metadata, and collect results concisely. For example, Files. walk(start). filter(p -> p. toString(). endsWith(". java")) will yield all Java files beneath a tree. Streams returned by Files. list and Files. walk must be closed either explicitly or by using try-with-resources to avoid resource leaks. A common misconception is treating Files. walk as lazy without closing it; leaving the stream open can hold file handles.
